utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-T. The Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is public open session and in open session I would like to welcome everyone in this courtroom, now to be the representatives of the OTP. I also welcome Mr. Seselj and our new legal officer who just started, and who is in this courtroom for the first time. I also welcome our Registrar, our usher, and our court reporter, as well as the interpreters helping us. Before giving the floor to Mr. Seselj who has three matters to raise, I would like to tell him right away the following: Last week there was no hearing, the Trial Chamber believed that the two witnesses that were scheduled to be withdrawn, and the Trial Chamber made a Scheduling Order requesting the OTP to give the schedule for five witnesses and the schedule has been circulated to each and every one. I believe that you have obtained it also, Mr. Seselj. The Trial Chamber will rule after having received your written submissions as to the request made by the OTP to stay the proceedings, the Trial Chamber is asking you, Mr. Seselj, to send us your written submissions as fast as possible so that the Trial Chamber can make its decision in light of the OTP's written submissions as well as your own submissions. This is a very important topic, and we need to render a written decision on this. I believe that this will be a crucial decision. So, Mr. Seselj, we are waiting for your written submissions in this respect because you are the first one involved here. Now, maybe this is what you wanted to talk about, so I will give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all I'd like to say something that I hadn't planned to say with respect to what you've just said, Mr. President. And I'll make your job easier straightaway. I'm not going to tender any written submission. I'm absolutely astounded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, I believe that there is a problem, I do not have French interpretation. I did not receive French interpretation. There may be a problem with the channels. French is on 5 normally. Could French interpreters please talk on the French channel, on channel 5. Very well, they were -- they are in the Albanian booth, actually, so everything is fine. Mr. Seselj, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the fact that for a full four months, I have not been able to have normal cooperation a my legal advisors given the fact that this is how I've been preparing in order to appropriately conduct the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses, especially those enjoying protective measures, I have no choice but to use documents submitted to me by the OTP. Again, I must tell you this, the Prosecutor has not been particularly conscientious with this, and they have not been keeping up with their documents and with their disclosure obligations. There is a witness who is bound to appear in the courtroom. Their duty is to forward to me all the transcripts of all the evidence provided by that witness in previous trials. In this case the witness testified in the single trial, the Milosevic trial, the transcript was submitted to me based on a book published by Natasa Kandic in Belgrade. The parts of his evidence given in closed session are missing. And then the Prosecutor submits to me these closed session transcripts on the 18th of March last year. A total of 20 pages of the record. I have them in front me as we speak as a matter of fact. Now I've been comparing them to the open session transcript, and I have just reached the conclusion that there are pages missing over the weekend. Between 18656 and 18662, six pages missing. So we have 18, the first two digits always, and then 663 to 665 missing again. 684 to 691, missing. 694 to 695, missing. There, anyone can have a look for themselves, anyone can have a look at what I got from the Prosecutor and can see for themselves what exactly is missing. Next thing, tomorrow the witness is about to appear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I will try and settle this problem. I'm a little bit surprised by what you are saying, Mr. Seselj. If the Prosecution discloses to Mr. Seselj a transcript of what the witness may have said in another trial, in that case, you are given all the pages on the transcript. How can pages be missing? Mr. Mundis, I find it difficult to understand this. Mr. Mussemeyer also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just give us a few moments if you would. My case manager is diligently checking our records to determine what exactly is disclosed, and if, in fact, there is a gap in any of the page numbers. But it might take her a few moments to run through all those page ranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation of what Mr. Mundis said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me translate what he has just said, he just said that they are currently checking with their case manager what documents have actually been disclosed to you. You will be told very shortly. What is the second point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now for something that I find exceptionally important in relation to tomorrow's witness. I think he is not a protective witness, but it doesn't matter because I wasn't about to mention his name anyway. Names don't matter to me. You know full well that I challenge the fact that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party would have been sent to Samac. However, some members of the Serbian Radical Party were involved in the fighting in Samac, that much is true. And they were involved in the units of the JNA. Among them Srecko Radovanovic who had undergone special training because he had an outstanding record in Slavonia as a volunteer. So he arrived with a unit that was part of the 17th tactical group. They arrived in Samac. Now, the Prosecutor had an obligation to submit to me the evidence of Slavko [indiscernible] in his capacity as a suspect. They submitted this to me on the 8th of July, 2008, which is the first day of the interview the 17th of January 2003. I had not previously had an opportunity to go through this. I only have now in preparation for this testimony. I see that the next day is missing of the interview. I have 52 pages in relation to day one of the interview, and I see that this continues on the following day, but I have nothing on the following day. I've gone through all the documents, and I haven't found this yet, perhaps it was disclosed to me later on. So they should speak up and say whether they have, in fact, disclosed this or not, but I don't have it. And I believe they were under obligation to disclose this to me in its entirety. Quite aside from the fact that the Aleksandar Vasiljevic interview hasn't been disclose today me yet, Certain portions. Jovika Panic [phoen], same thing. All day at the beginning of last year, you told them explicitly to do just that and to comply. And now to top it all off on the 2nd of June, 2008, I received confirmation from the OTP that they were disclosing to me the statement of Srecko Radovanovic dated the 26th of November, 2002. Needless to say, I put this away in a certain folder, a folder about Srecko Radovanovic. And I don't read immediately everything I get from the OTP, but just as I see fit. Now, I'm preparing for tomorrow's witness, I pick up this document, and I realise that in the attachment what I find is not Srecko Radovanovic's statement. Now, we don't even know whether Srecko Radovanovic gave a statement like that because what I find in my attachment is a statement of Srecko Borisavljevic, a JNA officer, a totally different person. Here you can have it, your own expert can have a look and see this was stapled together. No interventions were made, no one even touched this. So instead of Srecko Radovanovic's statement dated the 2nd of June, 2008, what I get is Srecko Borisavljevic's statement. Am I suppose prepare for a trial like this? On the other hand, you take away my ability to prepare with the assistance of my legal advisors, when I would not need any documents at all. I'm now deprived of the assistance of my legal advisors, and on top of that being hampered by the OTP in preparing for trial by using methods such as the one that I've just specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, it seems that as far as tomorrow's witness is concerned VS-1010, that interviews are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as was the case with respect to the previously mentioned material. Our case manager is checking that, and we can certainly be in a position to update the Chamber and Mr. Seselj certainly during the course of this morning. I do want to put on the record, however, while I'm on my feet that the repeated statements by the accused that is his ability to represent himself is hindered, is not in our respectful view a truthful statement. And, of course, there are motions pending before this Chamber to alleviate this situation. But it is our view that having had access to his associate Mr. Aleksic that the accused should not be continuing to indicate that his ability to represent himself is hindered. We do want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, basically you were saying that it is difficult for you to self-represent yourself, and you have brought this on to yourself, so the Prosecutor has got up and said that that is the best evidence, that you should be assigned a counsel. Let's backtrack a little bit. A few minutes ago, you said you found it difficult. What prevented you from telephoning Mr. Aleksic and telling him, Well, during the week we have such and such a witness that is going to come and testify. Can you do what is asked of you? In other words, look up such and such an item. And then all the people working for you will get to work and make sure that Mr. Aleksic sends you the answers you have requested in due time. And you have said, No, you are not doing this because there is an obstruction to your Defence according to what you are saying. This is not -- your conversations are not tapped. You can say to him well, Witness 1010 is coming to testify. You give this gentleman your instructions, and then he gets to work. But you are saying I'm not doing this, so the Prosecution gets on his feet and says, Well, make sure that he has a counsel, and then the counsel will do --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I never said I was unable to defend myself. But rather, that the Prosecution was keeping me from defending myself and deliberately obstructing me and hindering me. I have led evidence to that effect. I'm able to defend myself even if the OTP never submit another document to me ever again. Even without a single associate ever in Belgrade. I'll still be able to defends myself, and I still remain far superior to a ten-man Prosecutor team. Far superior. But my Defence will not have the sort of quality that I would find desirable. What should I do with Boris Aleksic for example? He is not up to date. Some days ago his wife gave birth to is a child. The only thing I can do is use a landline to call him, which means call him at his flat. His wife is still frail. She has just given birth. And I am now call him. And yet he is helpless without Zoran Krasic. You, the Trial Chamber, banned me from forwarding any sort of confidential information at all to Zoran Krasic. If I am now banned from forwarding confidential information directly to Zoran Krasic, what does that mean? I could do it through Boris Aleksic. Perhaps I should call him up. I should dictate a statement to him, he could tape-record it, and hand it over to Zoran Krasic. Would that be fair and in keeping with the rules? If that is a fair course of action, if that is a way for me to circumvent your decision without causing any further consequences, well, perhaps I could that I can at that course. But Zoran Krasic, he is the only person who is privy to everything. And he really understands and knows the ins and outs of everything single thing. He has it all in his computer. How can I get any serious work done without him? Come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, as far as this particular point is concerned, you are partially right, but I shall ask the Registrar to move into closed session please. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a brief objection. I think that the witness should be asked whether he wishes to continue with protective measures or perhaps he is ready now to testify in public? I think there's no concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness -- let's move back to private session, first. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, the witness testimony Milosevic has been admitted in the Krajisnik case under Rule 92(D), just to inform Your Honour and the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please let us know where you are from and where you went to school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: I'm from the environs in Bijeljina; that's where I was born. I went to school in my native (redacted). I then went to secondary school in Bijeljina, and I lived in Bijeljina until the outbreak of the conflict in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did you do after you finished your school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: After I finished secondary school, I did my military service in Slovenia and having done my military service, I went to Sarajevo to the school for Internal Affairs, and I trained as a policeman, to become a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you finished your training, what was your first duty station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: My first duty station was the police station in Bijeljina. Yes, the police station in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I now intend to go to the years 1991. Mr. Witness, can you tell us if there was a kind of rising tensions between the different ethnicities in your region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, directly in the area in which I lived somewhat less, but in the Republic of Croatia and around Bosnia, it was evident that there was tension between the different groups of different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: In 1991, the end of the summer, beginning of autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What were the facts from which you concluded that there was raising tensions? Could you describe this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: At that time I was coming back from my holidays, and I had spent my holiday around Zadar and Split. And while I was travelling back from Split in the direction of Bihac, I would come across -- I would go across Croatian territory where there had already been the erection of barricades, barricades had already been erected and meetings by the national groups had already been organised, rallies. And a few days later a conflict broke out in that part of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who erected these barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: In the area that I passed through, it was mostly areas inhabited by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you realise kind of, let's call it nationalistic rallies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mussemeyer, I appreciate your attempts to get to the point, but please don't try and lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It's not my intention to lead the witness, but these are points which are not crucial for the accused, and I want to go quickly through. So I ask the witness if he can answer my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, if you are asking -- if you are putting the question to him by saying, Do these rallies have a nationalist connotation, I believe that you are very leading there, but move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like the witness to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that area of the Republic of Croatia, these nationalistic meetings or rallies were organised, and I can state now that they were organised by, I think the Serb party or some Serb party in that region inhabited predominantly by a Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have there also been discussions or debates between your police colleagues?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, after those events there was a division among us too, who was for, who was against, who was right, who was wrong, so you could foresee that it would happen among our ranks very quickly, a division between us colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where did these -- or where did you observe or hear these discussions? Was it in a group? Or was it in a different place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, it began first of all along the channels that we used for communication in the police force. That is to say, you could hear discussions between colleagues in the neighbouring republic, the Republic of Croatia, so that we followed those conversations, and automatically, where we were, you could notice a division among us because our colleagues who were Serbs, our Serb colleagues who until recently -- well, the paperers that were published in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnian papers, automatically were being read -- well, they read newspapers from Belgrade, and they didn't read the Bosnian or Croatia papers. They refused to read them, but only read papers from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did police officers from Muslim origin also participate in these discussions? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: No, no. I remember very well, as far as I know from where I worked, we didn't interfere -- well, we didn't interfere, colleagues didn't interfere from other ethnicities except for one outbreak when a channel was opened, one station had their communication channel open, and you could hear two colleagues discussing these matters. And they were Serbs by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember a special event when the situation deteriorated tremendously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: At that time a conflict broke out, well, there was a clash, not a major one, large scale, but anyway, a clash in the villages between the Bratunac municipality or the surrounding parts of Bratunac. Well, in actual fact a Muslim man was killed. He was shot at in a car, and after that incident there was great discord and unrest between the two ethnic group, the Muslims and the Serbs. They were opposite each other. So we had to be sent to that region afterwards, we were sent there to separate the two sides, or the two villages, or actually, it was a number of villages, but villages with different ethnic groups living in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How would you describe the situation between the different ethnicities at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, at that time in that area, the area to which we were sent, you had the Serbs and the Muslims, and they lived opposite each other. For example, they were just divided by the road, and I can say that they were armed so that every time we were sent there, if we got close to one side or the other side, we had to change our names. If you are -- if you were going to Serb village, then you would have a Serb name. If you went to a Muslim village, you would take on a Muslim name, so that they weren't able to see which ethnicity we belonged to, but this was a little difficult to keep up because we were in between two fires, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you are saying something important here. There's an incident, a Muslim is killed, the police forces and you were part of them, go and try to separate the two sides. But you are adding -- they were armed. So why is it that at the time the authorities didn't decide to just arrest the perpetrators of this murder and ask everyone to surrender their arms, maybe sending in the army to try to restore law and order? Why wasn't this done? When there's a fire being lit, you try to put it out immediately. You know, if you don't put it out quickly, everything burns. So why wasn't anything done to restore law and order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why nothing was done? Well, I can't really say now. First of all, we didn't receive any orders to that effect to intervene at all in any one of those villages. And all the population there was armed. Now, who they got their weapons from, I can't say, but there was no order from our superior command telling us to intervene. If we were to come across people who were armed that way and to disarm them, so we had no possibility of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you remember a conversation you overheard over the police radio between two Serb police officers? And what were they telling about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, those two colleagues were talking. Whether intentionally or not, they left the channel open, their communication line was open so that we could hear them, and the entire region used those communication channels. Anyway, they were discussing the situation in Croatia and what was happening in Croatia to the Serbs and to the Croats, and they said that Croats and Muslims in Bosnia would suffer the same fate, that the same thing would happen there, what happened in Bosnia would happen in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did this conversation have any consequences for the two police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did not. Although, you could clearly see which wavelengths were used for the conversations, but as far as I know there were no consequences. They weren't punished because of it, and it was all hushed up just as if nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you yourself experience problems at your work for the fact that you were of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, there were problems, mostly in -- if you were punishing somebody of a different ethnicity, Serb, for instance. Or if you had any contacts, if you happened to stop a person who was in the reserve force of the army or was a member of the army, well, then, they would abuse you, tell you you couldn't do anything, you couldn't punish them in any way, and they said that you were just trying to punish them because they were Serbs. So problems of that kind occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what about your superiors? Were they of all ethnical background, or were they of a single ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From various ethnicities, but mostly the commander would be one ethnicity, the deputy would be another, and so on. It was always a mixed composition until 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a bit surprising. In Yugoslavia at that time, it was quite normal for the police to see civilians with weapons? That was quite normal at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we were to undertake anything, if we were to do anything, well, if you happened to come across some weapons in somebody's car or somebody having weapons on them without the documents required, then the weapons that we would seize would be returned to that same person one or two days later because, and I remember this very well, with a colleague of mine -- well, a colleague of mine confiscated a weapon from somebody who was going to Serbia via Croatia and when searching his car, they found a pistol and a hunting rifle and a knife, and he didn't have permits for those weapons. But when we seized those weapons, two days later, all this was returned to him because they got permits from somewhere. They came in with a permit from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you always work at Bijeljina, or were you also sent to other locations in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Mostly in Bijeljina, but from time to time when the need arose, they could send us to anywhere in the former Yugoslavia. So it didn't matter whether you wanted to or not, that was the law governing Internal Affairs. For example, the federal SUP or the republican SUP could say, I need five men from Bijeljina today to go somewhere else. So I was sent to Bratunac, for example, and then afterwards to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to come back to these weapons. Either, you know, inhabitants have their fighting -- or their hunting rifle, Okay, this is understandable. In the countryside people usually have hunting rifles, or on the other hand, they have war weapons. And if that's the case, how did they get them? Because you seem to say that some organisations provided them with weapons, Muslims, Serbs, or Croats. So were there really organisations who provided weapons to all these people? I mean, you know, an assault rifle is expensive. If someone has a weapon, either he was given the weapon or he bought this weapon. Could you tell us what was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it depends on the type of the weapon. The weapons that were prohibited were automatic weapons mostly. You could purchase hunting rifles yourself, but only if you had the necessary documents when going to buy one, whereas the other kind of weapons were not accessible to the civilian population, the automatic weapons and so on. And I can tell you, as far as I know, that the population, the Serb population, would receive weapons from the JNA. Whether it was directly from the JNA or the Territorial Defence, the TO, whereas the Muslim population, well, allegedly, I heard that they purchased the weapons. Now, where they bought them from, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you remember if you have been sent to another location by the end of February or beginning of March 1992, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: To Bosanski Samac, to secure the bridge in Bosanski Samac in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how was the relationship between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims there, at Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that all these groups were already divided, each group for themselves, and then passing through the villages in that area, inhabited by different ethnicities, each village would have a check-point set up by the locals of the village. So we had to pass through these checkpoints that were manned by the locals. It wasn't the soldiers, they were the locals, but they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was it possible for you to go into a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: No, no, not into the villages, but to pass by the villages, I was allowed to do that. I could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Starting from this, it seems that there's no more law and order, it's anarchy. If police is no longer allowed to enter into a Serb village, there must be a real problem then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. At the time if somebody had a rifle in their hands, they had greater power than the police. And to stand up to someone like that, you just cause greater conflicts. So we didn't dare react to things like that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what kind of caps your police officers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, we were there, well, to prevent any more conflicts. And mostly we had ordinarily caps, knitted caps, just to keep you from the cold. Whereas our Serb colleagues refused to wear caps like that, and they wore the Tito-type of cap with the five-pointed star. The normal police caps that were standard issue at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What emblem did you have on your cap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know why the Serb officers were wearing the cap with the five-pointed star?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Mussemeyer. The witness's answer to your question of which emblem they wore on their cap was not recorded. Could you put the question to him again, the answer well recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, which kind -- do you know why the Serb colleagues were wearing the cap with the five-pointed star?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, mostly to provoke the Croatian side. The colleagues from the Republic of Croatia who were stationed halfway up the bridge. Well, we were at the one end of the bridge, and they were halfway across the bridge in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go now to the events in Bijeljina. I think it's a good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. I still did not understand which emblems they wore themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I understood that they didn't wear any emblem, but it's up to the witness to explain us again of what kind of emblems did you have on your caps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think it would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I would like to welcome Mrs. Dahl who has just joined us. I shall give the floor back to Mr. Mussemeyer, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, before the break we were talking about Bosanski Samac, that you had been ordered to go there. Now, I would like to come to the events in Bijeljina. Can you tell us, how did you become aware of problems in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: While I was at work, while I was doing my job in Bosanski Samac, I saw that some conflict had broken out in Bijeljina on television, and that evening the commander, the chief of the police station in Bijeljina, called us and said that my colleague and I should return to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you do this and did you find any problems while returning to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: The next day there was a car that was placed at our disposal, and a colleague who worked there was supposed to transport us in the car, and when we returned to Bijeljina -- well, from Brcko to Bijeljina, on that stretch of the road, we came across a number of barricades that had been erected along the road and we were stopped and checked each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who had erected these barricades, and who stopped you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: The population of those villages, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many barricades you had to go through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: I think about 17 barricades up to the entrance to Bijeljina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And you finally arrived to Bijeljina, did you find any problems at the outskirts of Bijeljina or could you directly go into Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: At the last barricade at the entrance to Bijeljina, or just before you enter Bijeljina, we were stopped by a number of people at the barricade, and they checked us, and after that a car had to come from our own police station to drive us to the police station itself escorted by them. They wouldn't let us go on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who were they? Were they soldiers, and if so, from which unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: The regular -- no, no, they weren't regular soldiers. They were the reservists of the JNA. And the civilian population which lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember what one of these reservists asked your Serb colleague who was driving you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: He asked me why he was driving me, and after that they had to send a car for us from the station to escort me, not him, for security reasons. And all he said was that we had been given instructions from the commander that we should be in -- well, we were in Samac and our commander, the chief of police, told us to go back to the station urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What do you think why he was asking this, your Serb colleague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Because he knew that I was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you entered the town, what did you see and realise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: When I entered the town, I noticed that there was a large number of soldiers in the town already of para-military units wearing all sorts of different uniforms. And one could notice that there had been clashes. It wasn't before later on that I realised what exactly had occurred, once I had reached the station already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you realise kind of obstacles on the streets in Bijeljina, and if so, please describe it to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: In several places that I passed there were barricades, obstacles, cars and trucks parked across the road. I don't know who put them there, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mussemeyer, could you just clear with the witness exactly when it was he entered the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify it, but I can do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate date when you were going back to Bijeljina and entered the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: The day after the clashes broke out, on or about the 1st of April. That's when I arrived. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you returned to the police station, did you have to sign some documents expressing your loyalty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes. We were made to sign -- I don't know exactly, but a document of loyalty to the Serbian SUP, S-U-P . I think it was called --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, while the witness is thinking about what exactly it was that he signed, I believe there's a need for the Trial Chamber to intervene regarding the leading questions by Mr. Mussemeyer. There was no there is no oath, that is obvious if we look at any of the witness's statements. He signed an agreement to the effect that he would be serving with the police of Republika Srpska. Mr. Mussemeyer is deliberately driving the witness to say that this was an oath. Notwithstanding the fact that the witness himself is setting the record straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, I believe it's on page 43, lines 7 and 8 where you say, you mention loyalty. I don't see to what extent this could be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I don't understand this. I was not talking about an oath. I was explicitly using the word "signing" the document of loyalty and was not talking about oath. So I don't understand where this should lead or be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was the interpretation both the witness and I got, an oath, and then the witness set the Prosecutor straight by saying this was no oath. So we might be talking at cross purposes, talking to Mr. Mussemeyer and the interpreter at the same time. Perhaps the Trial Chamber should say who exactly we should be listening to, the interpreter or Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor put a question on a document about loyalty. He didn't mention an oath, and it is the accused who mentions an oath. This is how I see things. Irrespective of this, Witness, Mr. Seselj has just said something which you need to clarify. Mr. Seselj has said that you signed an agreement with the police of the Republika Srpska. What does this mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true. This was an agreement that I signed about loyalty to the SUP, S-U-P, of Republika Srpska. I think it was called the Centre of the SAO Semberija, Majevica Services, I think that's what it was called, but it was about signing one's loyalty to, for example, the SUP of Republika Srpska because it wasn't Republika Srpska at the time, it was the Serbian MUP, M-U-P, at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you were a civil servant in the police of what country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The republican SUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but at the moment the republican SUP no longer got any respect among the Serbs, and there were no communications between the republican SUP and, for example, the Bijeljina station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment I would like the interpreters to be extremely careful. There is a mistake here. The witness said I was working for the SUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on page 44, line 24, it is said the SUP of the Republika Srpska. That's not what he said. So please repeat. I'm asking you this question, at that time you were a civil servant working for the police. For which country were you working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Republican SUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina up until that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we have it, I must just check that it is properly recorded on the transcript. And now you are being asked to sign an agreement with the SUP of the Republika Srpska. What did this mean? That Bosnia-Herzegovina did no longer exist, that there was a new republic, what did all of this mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that at the time there was a division within the republican SUP or in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The ethnic Serbs seceded from the others. We were not the first police station to do this, there had been other divisions before. A Serbian SUP or something like that was set up, or a SUP of Republika Srpska, but I don't think it was Republika Srpska. Therefore at the time we had the centre of security services, SAO Semberija, and Majevica and we signed our loyalty to that centre, because in Bosnia-Herzegovina all the SUPs were subject to security centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need to go more slowly. This legal concept can be very important and have consequences. First of all, you talked about the SUP of the Republika Srpska. Now you are saying something different. You are saying that you were part of the SUP of the SAO and then you said something else, so please clarify this again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked at the Bijeljina public security station, used to. Then it was the security services centre Tuzla that was in charge of us. And then when the clashes broke out in 1992 and whatever happened in Bijeljina, the Bijeljina security station seceded and a new security services centre was established. SAO Semberija, and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones be switched off while the witness is speaking, please, because the interpreters can't hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, were there Muslim police stations that were staffed by Muslims and were there police stations that were staffed by Croatians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in my area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An objection, just to make this easier. The witness is talking about what he was supposed to do following the clashes in Bijeljina once the Muslim forces had been defeated and had already withdrawn from Bijeljina. Therefore, Bijeljina now remains in the hands of the Serb forces. And then he signs his loyalty in order to keep working with the police. It's not very likely that was SAO Semberija, and Majevica, because Republika Srpska already existed. SAO Semberija, and Majevica had been set up the previous year, 1991. In April 1992 Republika Srpska very much existed already. Therefore it's much likelier that he signed his loyalty in order to keep on working with the police of Republika Srpska. However, the Prosecutor would have encountered no problems in making sure the document was available for us and this is no secret at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you agree with the fact that you signed a document in order to work for the SAO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Seselj adds that this SAO existed prior to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't agree. All right. Not officially. But did it exist de facto?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It was important to clarify this. Mr. Mussemeyer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what was your task when you were back to the police station? Did you get a specific task?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes, the first day we got an order, all of us, to not leave the station. It wasn't before day two, I think, that I got an order from my boss that I should go into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What were you expected to do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: I and my colleague who came with me were expected to escort or secure persons who were picking up the bodies of dead civilians and soldiers. Those who were killed on the streets of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your task during this, let's call it exercise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Securing the two persons who drove the two hearses and also remaining in touch with the station because we were receiving from the duty officer at the station all the locations that we were to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you perform this work without being harassed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: No, not quite that simple. There were many soldiers and paramilitaries, to put it that way, around town. People who stopped us, checked us, let us go. There were some disarming going on later on. All sorts of things happening over the two days that I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know to which units these paramilitaries belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Oh, well, Arkan's army, for example, the JNA reservists, and some people organised by Mirko Blagojevic, volunteers. A mixed bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did these paramilitaries tell you what was going on in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: They were saying that these people had been killed as a result of war, although there had been no war at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you -- please explain us why there was no war, according to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Well, the word "war" implies large scale clashes. The use of all sorts of weaponry such as shelling, bombing, and so on and so forth. As far as I could notice, small arms and light weapons were used for the killing of those people. Automatic rifles at best, I think. Sometimes the occasional Zolja, and there was no major damage resulting from those clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many bodies you helped collecting in these days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were about 48 bodies that I collected. I can also say that there were a lot more, but there were some bodies that I was supposed to collect, that had been collected by their families before I got there and were buried secretly in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Witness. Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the document under 65 ter 2702 on the monitor, please. And this is under seal. Maybe we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, I have a question first for the witness. Witness, would you also say that there was no civil war underway? No internal conflict at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say it was war. Clashes between ethnicities, for example, the Muslims and the Serbs who were in town, yes, there were clashes. That much was obvious. But as for the use of some weapons such as shelling and that sort of thing, not exactly on a large scale. This was mere the exchange of rifle fire going on for a day or two, and then it was all done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we move to private session, please, because we have to display a document under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you know some of the victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which ethnicity they had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: The ones I knew were Muslims, but there were other ethnicities among the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you accompanied a person on the second day of your collection? Can you tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes, I was dispatched to escort an inspector from the federal SUP, from Belgrade, who had arrived from Belgrade. We were to welcome him on the way out of Bijeljina in the direction of Bosanska Raca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you go with him through the city without any problems, or have there been problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: When we returned after we met him, we were stopped near the barracks or near the Belimi cafe, I think that was what it was called, by the paramilitaries, I can't call them anything else because I don't know which unit they belonged to. Both I and my colleague were disarmed as well as the inspector who was driving a different car right behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you been disarmed? Yes, you told us, sorry. Did you get your arms back later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Jelisic was adamant that I should be given back my weapon, and I was. The inspector and I were returned our weapons, but my colleague was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that these were para-military units. How are you able to establish a distinction between JNA special units, for instance, and paramilitaries? What leads you to say that this is the official army and these are paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regular military units, there were none in the town. The reservists and in Yugoslavia, as it's well known, everybody had a reserve military uniform. So many people were actually wearing those, reserve uniforms. 50/50. Part uniform, part plain clothes, normally. But then, for example, Arkan's unit, they were wearing full combat gear with uniform, and they looked very much like an organised unit, while the others were loose cannons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like additional detail. When you are saying reserve military units, for you, are they legal units? Do these people belong to an army or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me, they were paramilitaries because they had not been mobilised by the military leadership which means that they had been mobilised by the Serbian Democratic Party and some other organisation like that, but not by the military, the army's leadership. They were not mobilised by the army's leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that Arkan's units had uniforms. Could you tell us which uniforms they were wearing? JNA uniforms or others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, yes, JNA or not JNA. Camouflage uniforms, full kits. You could buy a JNA uniform if you wanted to. It was available, but the boots, the trousers, the jacket, and a full combat kit. Normally what a JNA soldier would have had in those conditions, not including the military cap. These people were wearing knitted caps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, Mr. Mussemeyer, without giving you instructions or anything, we might have a photograph that could illustrate what the witness just said. Photograph 1037. You could ask for it to be displayed, and that way the witness could confirm what he said in his answer to Judge Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Okay. I agree. I had foreseen this photograph for some seconds later, but we can show it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we please have item 1037 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We have already seen this photo with another witness, and it has got the Exhibit number P684.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what kind of soldiers can we see here? To which unit do they belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: These are members of Arkan's unit, and as we can see, they are in full combat kit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you say as where, in which location in Bijeljina was this photo taken or where the victims are shown? Where is the location? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: The location is near the hospital, near Redzep's house. The person lying on the ground is Redzep, his wife, and a third person that I can't identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if also Redzep's child was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes. The child is across the way behind this first soldier's back, in the front yard of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Redzep's wife, could you tell us which lady it is on this photograph? Is it the body that is in the middle, or is it the body that's to the very right of the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. Very well. But you are telling us that Arkan's men were dressed in such a uniform, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Beanie cap, glasses, rangers on their foot, camouflage unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is something like it, but for the most part, they were in full combat kit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one who is with his foot raised, I see that on his back, slung across his back he has got something, seems to be a rocket-launcher. What do you think of it? Did they have rocket-launchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a Zolja, a small calibre rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you help collecting these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were these all the bodies you collected from that spot, or did you have to collect others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: No, behind this gate in front of Redzep's house, there are another four bodies, and then yet another four in the basement of Redzep's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you initially find these bodies in the basement, or did you have to be called back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: No. First I picked up the four bodies that were out in the street, and then I went to get the four bodies that were in the yard. I was afraid that the house itself, Redzep's house, or the basement might be booby-trapped, therefore, I didn't dare to actually go in and check. But later Mr. Redzep's relative, the Redzep who had been killed, reported that there were another four dead bodies in the basement of that house, so we went and got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you know one of these victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: A single one whose body was in the basement. Coso Nargalic, his body was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was him? Do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: It was difficult to recognise the other bodies there. The body was -- the head was defaced from the blows. It was disfigured, it was very difficult to make a positive ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you collected the bodies of these victims. On this photograph here, these civilians obviously had no weapon. I would like to know whether all the bodies that you collected were bodies of people with weapons or without weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. None of the persons whose bodies I collected were armed or had any military kit on them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a small mystery which I tried to raise, to unveil with another witness, but he was not able to answer. Maybe you won't be able to answer either. This is a photograph, it was taken by someone just when this soldier is about to -- obviously to kick the victim. Who took this picture? Is it one of Arkan's men, or is it freelance photograph that would be on the site at the time? Do you have any idea who took this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was a journalist. This photograph was taken from the direction of the hospital, and the person taking the photograph was probably concealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you collected these bodies, was somebody filming what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In this very spot shown in this photograph, I, as a matter of fact, tried to use my own camera, the one that I had in my car, but it was seized, and I was banned from taking any photographs or, indeed, checking the dead bodies. Their identities, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who took away your camera? You see, as we put the questions the witness, we learn a lot of things. Who actually took the camera away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's say it was Arkan's men. Members of Arkan's unit. They were wearing the same sort of -- the outfit as the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there was the police, but with the police, were there other people collecting these bodies alongside the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what exactly you mean, but with me there were another two persons from the public utilities company. They were seconded by the company to help collect the bodies. I didn't, myself, collect the bodies. I provided security for those two people from the public securities party who actually did. And they were in charge of transporting these dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is exactly what I wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, it's 12.00. I believe it would be time for the break. We will finish at 1.15 today, so let's have a 15-minute break. And when we resume, it would be nice if the Registrar can tell me how much time you've already spent. Fifteen-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you remember having collected also the corpse of of a father and two sons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes, I do. About 300 metres away from the hospital towards Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who killed these victims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: As far as I know when I arrived later, I learned that those three people were killed by Brano Sumar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who was Brano Sumar, to which unit did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Brano Sumar, as far as I know, belonged to the Mirko Blagojevic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show a document. It's a document under seal, and we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to show a short video-clip now which has the 65 ter number 6010, and it deals with clip E. For your information, this clip has already been shown at our first video day. You will certainly remember the 20th of March, 2008, but it was -- for an error of the Prosecution, it did not get a P number. It was not admitted. We thought that this video-clip was already admitted with the Milosevic testimony of Mr. Seselj and had the P number 56, but clip A got the number P56. And now I want to see again clip E. It's a very short video, and I ask to get it admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you recognise Mirko Blagojevic on this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask to get this video-clip admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Before we rule on this, sir, did you hear like I did -- this was shown very quickly. I believe he said, "I'm the President of -- I'm the regional President of the Serbian Radical Party." Did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the person saying that was Blagojevic, Mirko Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we see -- at some point we see a building which is marked "Gogo". Is this in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from the first sketch where I marked the cafe bar Istanbul and the cafe bar Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we see two sets on this video-clip. We hear the fighting; we hear the shooting. And this is shot live, so to speak. And then we have the interview of Blagojevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can hear the shots, the bursts of fire, but we have the feeling that no one is firing back. Is that what you heard also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On a number of occasions there was shooting without any reason hitting shops, houses, just like that. Nobody was in any of those buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, could we see the video-clip again and stop when Blagojevic is speaking so that we can see the insignia he is wearing and what he is wearing because it moves on so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he says, I'm the President of the regional -- of the Serbian Radical Party -- "I'm the regional President of the Serbian Radical Party." So you saw him on the picture. When you saw him, was he dressed like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he wasn't dressed like that. I didn't see him looking like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he wasn't dressed like that, oh. What was different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the interpretation. Could you say it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat my question. What was different? What is different between what we see and between what you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: Normally, he didn't have a uniform, but here we have to see -- well, that the members of the unit led my Mirko Blagojevic, that they all had these cockades on their heads, whereas the rest didn't have those, for example, the reservists, the JNA reservists, or Arkan's unit, they didn't have cockades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give this an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor is repeating the same mistake that he made in March last year. He is not telling us the date when this was filmed because the fighting in Bijeljina lasted four days. In the document attached to this file, it says that it's a statement by Vojvoda Blagojevic in Bijeljina March 1992. There was no fighting in March. The fighting began on the 31st of March and went on for at least the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd of April. So we need dates and possibly who filmed this so that we know what day this was filmed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, where do these pictures come from? What is the date of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The exact dates, I cannot tell you. I don't know. I can tell you how the Prosecution received this video-clip. I already mentioned it in March. We received it from Sonja Biserko, and the date was the 6th of November, 2002, that she gave it to the Prosecution. More, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we have the video-clip, we need an Exhibit number. Mr. Registrar please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P737.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was informed, if you see at this still at the left-hand corner at the top, there is the Logo of a Serbian television. From Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this is a question of a technical nature. When Blagojevic says we are controlling all the exits and entrances to the town, we have the feeling that he is the big boss. He is in charge of everything. He gives an interview to television. Was that the case or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That he was keeping everything under control, I don't believe that. The Crisis Staff was in charge of that, after all. They were holding all the access roads into the town. Well, that was the case even before the clashes broke out. I can only say that the clashes went on for about two days, meaning between the 31st and the 1st. On the 1st and perhaps early on the 2nd of April. After that there were no clashes. No shooting. Shooting into the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if you say that the clashes lasted two days, this means that the Muslim forces fought? There was fighting in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there fighting? There was probably someone, but it wasn't to the same extent. For example, there was no unit that was holding the entire centre of town because there was no such thing. So there were no major clashes. Individual, sporadic clashes, two or three men involved who were armed and then they fired at a member of this unit, that unit, Arkan's unit, but not to any major extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims that were shooting at Arkan's men, were these Muslims placed under anybody's command, or were they just doing what they felt like doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was no command. For example, some neighbourhoods organised themselves, and that's how resistance was put up. Based on that. I'm not aware of there being any direct command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about you, yourself? Maybe this question would have been put during cross-examination. You were a Muslim policeman. Normally speaking, your side would have been the Muslim side. Why didn't you shoot at Arkan's men and the other men? Or did you shoot and you are not talking about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I wasn't shooting myself. If I had been shooting, I would have been killed, that much is certain. I said already and I'll say it again, I was at the police station, and the entire station was not involved in the clashes that were going on in the town. I simply had no opportunity to clash with those persons at all. But I know that on day three, I went into town myself. I was walking around. There was no shooting, no actions, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question mark. Arkan's men saw you, and they didn't kill you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But when I was walking around town, they couldn't know who I was and what I was doing, especially Arkan's men, since at the time I was wearing a beret with a Serb three-coloured flag which led them to believe that I, too, was Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. This was important. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, was it possible for the civilian inhabitants of Bijeljina to leave the town whenever they wanted after April 1991, or did they need specific permission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Anyone leaving the town, especially for Serbia needed a permit from the Crisis Staff or from what was then the TO staff. The recruitment office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show such a -- it is called freedom of movement pass, but we have to go into private session because it's a document under seal. Mr. Registrar, I would like to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know -- or what do you know about the destroyed mosque in Bijeljina? Can you confirm that some of them have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes, mosques were destroyed. I think long after the clashes had broken out. They were destroyed in areas where there were no combat operations at all. Bijeljina and the entire region, and I'm referring to Muslim settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have the document under number 880 on the 65 ter list shown on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, I would like to ask you if you know -- can tell us which mosque it is? Do you know this place? And can you please let us know which mosque it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: Yes. This is near Bijeljina, not -- an area that was not affected by any war operations at all. Booby-trapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, when? Mr. President, yes, booby-trapped, yes, destroyed, but when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you a specific date, but it was destroyed in 1992. And this place is about 15 kilometres from the frontline where there was fighting. This is a Muslim village which was later settled by Serbs, therefore, there were no operations anywhere nearby. It was booby-trapped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it was destroyed, could you tell us after which month it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could only have been autumn 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the fall of 1992. Very well. Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, was there fighting around Bijeljina after the spring also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No fighting around Bijeljina. All of the places around Bijeljina are predominantly Serb, settled, but there was only Janja in the direction of Zvornik. No clashes there at all. Villages towards Stajocuk, Janja, Bijeljina, Trnovo, likewise no clashes. In July all of the Muslims left those villages. They moved out. Although they had previously signed the statement of loyalty to SAO Semberija, and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P739.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the next photo on the monitors. It appears the 65 ter number 2763.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, when we can see it, please let us know which mosque it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is there a second page that we can see?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There's only one page, but two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Then, please, can you show us the next photo which bears the 65 ter number 2763. It's the same, I guess.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photo currently broadcast is 2763.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what do you see on the first picture at the top? This was the mosque you already described. And is it the same location which shown on the second picture at the bottom, and what does it show?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VS-1035
utterances.text: This is the mosque in the centre of Janja. The original condition. The upper photograph. And the lower photograph the ones that have been blown up by mines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are two different mosques, both are in Janja, but they are not one in the same mosque, and I think the Prosecutor should prepare a little better. In the first photograph the mosque that the witness is talking about without telling us when it's destroyed. The other photograph shows a different mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's put an end to this. So, Witness, please, when was the -- when was this destroyed with plastic explosives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This momentarily the same, they were all blown up at one period of time, but I can't be specific about the date because I wasn't there when they were destroyed. But I could see from a certain spot exactly when they vanished, but not the exact date, let's say, at the same time all the mosques in that region were destroyed. Late in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of 1992. Very well. I think we've been through this with the expert who came to testify on mosques. I wonder whether a decision has been actually handed regarding the admission of these pictures. But let's give it a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer, we have to put an end to this. We have to stop now because we have -- I have another hearing starting soon. I would like the Registrar to please tell me the time he spent already. You haven't used up a lot of time. You still have 30 minutes. But we'll have to move faster because tomorrow there's another witness scheduled. If we have constant objections, Mr. Seselj, we won't be able to hear the next witness. Ms. Dahl, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to put on the record that we located the missing closed session transcripts with regard to the witness. We had them transcribed into the Serbian language, and I've given copies to the Registrar to disclose to Mr. Seselj. We apologise for the oversight. Approximately 20 pages of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've given them to Mr. Seselj. Witness, you are now in the hands of justice, a witness of justice. You are not supposed to contact anyone except, of course, members of your family. You can just tell them that everything is going well. We will meet tomorrow at 8.30 in the morning. And I would like everyone tomorrow to be extremely concise and brief and fast because we have another witness scheduled, and if we don't finish with this one, the other witness will have to stay until next week. Have a pleasant afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of January 2009, at 8.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.13 p.m.
